title: CHEM 105 General Chemistry I
shortDescription: A 14-week first-semester general chemistry course grounded in college benchmarks and free chemistry sources.

sourceRecords.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 5.111 Principles of Chemical Science

scope.audience: Undergraduate science, health science, and engineering students taking first-semester general chemistry.
scope.level: Undergraduate introductory chemistry with college algebra readiness.
scope.duration: 14 weeks, equivalent to a 3-4 credit General Chemistry I course with lab-aware practice.
scope.outcome: Explain and solve foundational chemistry problems using measurement, atomic structure, bonding, reactions, thermochemistry, gases, kinetics, equilibrium, and acid-base reasoning.

content.heading: Explanation
content.value: This week develops matter and measurement as part of a first-semester college general chemistry sequence. The lesson starts from observable evidence, translates that evidence into chemical language, and then applies the relevant model to calculations or particle-level explanations. The treatment is source-backed: readings and examples are anchored to source-openstax-chemistry-2e, source-khan-chemistry-archive, while lab practice emphasizes measurement discipline, laboratory safety, and careful interpretation of data. The core connection is that chemistry moves between the macroscopic world of samples and instruments, the particulate world of atoms, ions, and molecules, and the symbolic world of formulas, equations, graphs, and units.

content.heading: Worked example
content.value: Worked example: a sample problem on matter and measurement begins by naming the chemical system, listing the measured quantities, and writing the governing relationship. The solution keeps units visible, checks whether the particle model fits the situation, and ends with an interpretation in plain language. For example, when matter appears in a calculation, the answer is not complete until the numerical result, significant figures, and chemical meaning agree with the given evidence.

content.heading: Practice
content.value: Practice: solve one calculation or explanation problem from the primary source, then create a short error check. The check must identify the known quantities, the chemical principle used, one possible misconception, and one safety or measurement concern. Finish by writing a two-sentence explanation that uses the terms matter, significant figures, unit conversion accurately.

The treatment is source-backed: readings and examples are anchored to source-openstax-chemistry-2e, source-mit-ocw-5111, while lab practice emphasizes measurement discipline, laboratory safety, and careful interpretation of data. The core connection is that chemistry moves between the macroscopic world of samples and instruments, the particulate world of atoms, ions, and molecules, and the symbolic world of formulas, equations, graphs, and units.

content.heading: Worked example
